title: Cracking 'Is this appropriate, and why?' items
blurb: Split every 'and why?' item into a verdict and a reason, decide the verdict from the scenario, then pick the one reason that explains it.
question: Two options say 'Yes, because...' and two say 'No, because...'. Every reason sounds like something from the Official Book. How do you find the single right answer?

teach.body: Each official Version 2 Practitioner sample paper carries 8 to 10 '..., and why?' items, most of them asking 'Is this an appropriate application of..., and why?'. They test the analyse criteria: judging how a practice, or a process, has been applied or tailored. The four options form a grid: two verdicts (yes, no) crossed with two reasons each. Exactly one verdict-and-reason pair is right, so every item is really two decisions: the verdict, then the reason.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile Practitioner syllabus v2.0, 2.1.3 and 3.1.2

teach.caption: In the official sample papers the order is Yes, Yes, No, No. Get the verdict right and you are choosing between two.

teach.h: Five steps for every 'and why?' item

steps.label: Read the situation
steps.sub: Process, who acted, what they did

steps.label: Name the test
steps.sub: The practice or process in quotes

teach.h: The verdict comes from the facts
teach.body: Compare what happened with the method: what the practice's artifacts are for, who does what, what a workshop topic covers, and the agile intent (self-management within tolerances, transparency, value). Use the stem's facts: fixed budget, team maturity, the process the project is in. Then test each surviving reason with 'this is right because...'. The winner names the rule the action follows or breaks.

teach.h: Why a wrong option is wrong

children.label: Reason is untrue in the method
Reason true but does not explain it

teach.caption: The true-but-irrelevant reason is a typical trap in the official samples.

teach.body: In starting up Fair Fares (scenario AS1), Larkspur Rail's draft project canvas lists 'a new app release delivered in each of three stages' as the main benefit. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice? No: a release is an output, and a benefit is a measurable improvement the business values, such as fewer staff hours spent checking claims. A rival 'No' reason, 'benefits are recorded in the benefits management approach', is wrong: expected benefits belong in the canvas.

teach.text: Watch for two business case traps. Tailor, never drop: the project canvas is the agile form of the business case, so 'the canvas replaces the business case' never justifies having no justification. And an output is not a benefit: a release, an app or an agile transformation plan produced by a pilot is scope, not a measurable improvement.

items: Four options = two verdicts x two reasons; one pair is right.
Decide the verdict from the stem's facts before reading the options.
The right reason is true in the method AND explains this situation.
Business case: canvas with three cases, MVP named, measurable benefits, early releases.
Process tailoring: check the activity or topic matches the process's purpose.

summary: You can now split an 'and why?' item into a verdict and a reason, decide the verdict from the scenario, and reject reasons that are untrue or do not explain the case. You can also judge whether a business case approach or a process tailoring decision is appropriate.

A.q: On an 'Is this appropriate, and why?' item about Larkspur Rail, Aled decides from the stem that the action was not appropriate. Of the two 'No, because...' options, one states a true rule from the Official Book that has nothing to do with the action described; the other names the rule the action breaks. What should he do?
options: Choose the reason with the most detail from the book
Reconsider his verdict, as both reasons are true rules
Choose the reason that names the rule the action breaks
Choose the reason that repeats a fact from the booklet
A.why: The right reason must be true and must explain this situation; a true rule that does not explain it is a distractor.

whyNot.0: Detail is not the test; a detailed true statement can still fail to explain the case.
whyNot.1: Distractors are often true statements, so that is no reason to doubt a well-founded verdict.
whyNot.3: Booklet facts can appear in any option; what matters is whether the reason explains the action.

A.q: In starting up Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares project, the commercial director, appointed as project executive, leads the creation of the project canvas from the mandate. The canvas sets out best-case, worst-case and expected-case scenarios and names Release 1 as the minimum viable product. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the canvas gives three cases and names the MVP
Yes, because the project manager owns the project canvas
No, because a business case needs a full written document
No, because the MVP should be named in the release map
A.why: The project canvas should outline best, worst and expected cases and identify the MVP so an exception can be raised if it is forecast late (Table 5.2, 6.3.2).

whyNot.1: The executive leads the project canvas; the project manager does not own it.
whyNot.2: The one-page project canvas is a suitable replacement for the business case document.
whyNot.3: The canvas must identify the MVP; the release map shows when releases happen.

A.q: In the project kickoff workshop for Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares project, each of the three delivery teams designs its own team dashboard, and the group then creates the project dashboard together. Is this an appropriate application of the 'initiating a project' process, and why?
options: Yes, because the board designs the project dashboard
Yes, because teams co-create dashboards to self-manage
No, because team dashboards are set up in team planning
No, because the PM should set one dashboard format for all
A.why: Team dashboards are co-created by each team in the kickoff workshop to support transparency and self-management, and the project dashboard is created there too (13.4.4.2, Table 13.8).

whyNot.0: The project dashboard is created together in the kickoff workshop; the board pulls information from it.
whyNot.2: Team dashboards are updated and reviewed in team planning, but they are created in kickoff.
whyNot.3: Dictating dashboards would undermine the self-management the kickoff workshop aims to build.

B.q: During initiation of Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares project, the chief product owner runs a workshop with app developers, a tester and two members of the passenger panel. Together they write four fictional personas based on passengers' needs, such as a daily commuter who is often delayed. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
options: Yes, because personas should reflect age and income bands
Yes, because they are fictional, needs-based and few in number
No, because personas belong to the quality practice
No, because personas should describe real, named passengers
B.why: Personas should be fictional, based on user needs not demographics, written in a cross-functional workshop and, for a new product, no more than five (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Personas are based on needs, not demographics such as age or income.
whyNot.2: Personas are a business case technique (6.4.1).
whyNot.3: Personas are kept fictional, which widens the room for innovation.

B.q: Larkspur Rail's project board, its agile coaches and business representatives meet in the agile enablement workshop during Fair Fares initiation. There they draft the agile transformation plan that will replace the change management approach. Is this an appropriate application of the 'directing a project' process, and why?
options: Yes, because the workshop is for the board and agile coaches
Yes, because the plan can replace the change management approach
No, because the plan is agreed in the project initiation workshop
No, because the Agilometer replaces the transformation plan
B.why: The agile transformation plan is produced in initiation, under the management approaches topic of the project initiation workshop; the agile enablement workshop reviews Agilometer risks (Table 13.5, Table 13.7).

whyNot.0: True that the workshop is for the board and agile coaches, but its topics are Agilometer review and risk, not the transformation plan.
whyNot.1: True that the plan can replace the change management approach, but that does not make this the right workshop.
whyNot.3: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working; it does not replace a transformation plan.

B.q: In Larkspur Rail's project initiation workshop, the project manager records the project-wide criteria that an epic must meet before work on it can begin under the 'management approaches' topic. Is this an appropriate application of the 'initiating a project' process, and why?
options: Yes, because management approaches are co-created there
Yes, because these criteria form the quality approach
No, because each team agrees these in team planning
No, because the project DoR is a topic of its own
B.why: Criteria an item must meet before work starts are the project Definition of Ready, which is a separate topic of the project initiation workshop (Table 13.7).

whyNot.0: True that management approaches are co-created there, but these criteria belong to the project DoR topic.
whyNot.1: The Definition of Ready is its own artifact, not part of the quality management approach.
whyNot.2: Project-level DoR and DoD are set in the project initiation workshop, not by each team.

C.q: During Stage 2 of Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares project, the data team's matching model falls behind and the release map forecasts that Release 1, named as the minimum viable product in the project canvas, will miss its month-four date. The project manager prepares an exception report for the board. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
options: Yes, because a late forecast MVP is grounds for an exception
Yes, because the CPO sets the time tolerance for each release
No, because the MVP date can flex like a Could have story
No, because the teams should swarm before any exception
C.why: The project canvas identifies the MVP so that an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be late (6.3.2).

whyNot.1: The board sets project tolerances; the CPO represents users and owns the project backlog.
whyNot.2: Time has zero tolerance, and the MVP is the minimum the business needs.
whyNot.3: Swarming suits a blocker inside an iteration; a forecast breach of tolerance is an exception.

C.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's project manager, new to agile, uses initiation to draw up detailed task-level plans for every iteration of all three click and collect releases, so the board can see each task in advance. Is this an appropriate application of the 'initiating a project' process, and why?
options: Yes, because detailed plans help a new manager control costs
Yes, because the release map is documented in initiation
No, because the CPO prepares the project plan for the board
No, because task plans are made for the next iteration in MPD
C.why: Initiation documents a high-level release map; detailed task-level planning happens for the next iteration in managing product delivery, in the team planning workshop (8.3.2, 13.6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Cost has zero tolerance either way; detailed early task plans do not suit agile delivery.
whyNot.1: True that the release map is documented in initiation, but it is high level, not task level.
whyNot.2: The project manager prepares the project plan; the CPO owns the project backlog.

C.q: Larkspur Rail's benefits management approach for Fair Fares plans a benefits review shortly after Release 1 goes live, to measure the fall in staff hours spent checking claims, with further reviews after later releases and after the project closes. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
options: Yes, because all benefits are confirmed before closure
Yes, because frequent releases allow benefits to come early
No, because benefits reviews take place after closure
No, because benefits are measured on the project dashboard
C.why: In agile, frequent releases are planned to enable early delivery of benefits, and the benefits management approach defines the reviews (6.3.1, 6.3.2).

whyNot.0: Most benefits are confirmed after closure; the approach rightly includes a post-project review.
whyNot.2: Many reviews follow closure, but iterative releases can realize some benefits during the project.
whyNot.3: The dashboard shows progress; benefits reviews are defined in the benefits management approach.

reteach.title: Think like a referee: decision first, then the rule
reteach.question: A referee first decides foul or no foul, then names the rule. How does that help with 'and why?' items?

blocks.body: Treat each item like a referee's call. First the call: was the action right or wrong, given the facts? Then the citation: which rule makes it so? A referee who calls a foul but cites the wrong rule is still wrong. In the exam, the right verdict with the wrong reason scores nothing.

items: Cover the options and say yes or no to yourself.
Uncover the two options with your verdict.
Ask of each: does this rule explain THIS action?

explain.h: Half the options go at once
explain.body: Two options share each verdict. Once you have decided the verdict from the facts, the other two options are out, whatever their reasons say.

test.q: Bethan reads an 'and why?' item about Larkspur Rail with two 'Yes, because...' and two 'No, because...' options. From the facts she is confident the action was appropriate. How many options can she rule out before comparing reasons?
options: One, the weakest of the four reasons
Three, keeping the most detailed reason
None, as every reason must be compared
Two, the options with the 'No' verdict
test.why: Deciding the verdict removes the two options with the other verdict, leaving two reasons to compare.

whyNot.0: The verdict removes two options at once, not one.
whyNot.1: Two options remain with her verdict; she must still compare their reasons.
whyNot.2: The opposite-verdict options can go without comparing their reasons.

steps.label: Output
steps.sub: One-tap claim screen in the app

test.q: Larkspur Rail's project manager is checking the benefits listed in the Fair Fares project canvas. Which entry is a benefit rather than an output or an outcome?
options: A one-tap pre-filled claim screen
Claim checking cut by 6,000 staff hours a year
Passengers claiming through the app
A model that matches tickets to live train running data
test.why: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome, valued by the investing organization.

whyNot.0: A screen in the app is an output of the project.
whyNot.2: Changed passenger behaviour is an outcome.
whyNot.3: The matching model is an output.

explain.body: All projects need business justification. In PRINCE2 Agile the business case is tailored, and the project canvas is a suitable replacement for the traditional document.

test.q: Larkspur Rail's executive wants Fair Fares' business justification in a short visual form the board and teams can read at a glance. Which artifact is the suitable agile replacement for the business case?
options: The project backlog
The release map
The project canvas
The project brief
test.why: The project canvas is the agile tailoring of the business case: vision, value, options, costs, users, scope, benefits and major risks on one page.

whyNot.0: The project backlog replaces the project product description.
whyNot.1: The release map serves as the project and stage plan.
whyNot.3: The project brief is kept as a separate product in PRINCE2 Agile.

explain.body: Controlling a stage normally starts after the project is authorized, but it can be used during initiation for large or complex projects.

test.q: A candidate is judging whether a project may use the controlling a stage process during its initiation stage. In which situation is this appropriate?
options: When the project is large or complex
When the executive is on extended leave
When the CPO has approved the release map
When a pilot project has a single team
test.why: The book allows controlling a stage during initiation for large or complex projects.

whyNot.1: The executive's absence does not change which processes apply in initiation.
whyNot.2: The release map is approved by the board, and its approval does not trigger this.
whyNot.3: A small single-team pilot is the opposite of the large or complex case.
